text.en: Shemitah is Yerushalayim in time: the constant Shabbos that Yerushalayim holds in place spreads in the seventh year over the whole land.
A person may do melachah in Shemitah because the Shabbos of that year belongs to the ground, not to the person.
The laws that Yerushalayim was not divided among the tribes and may not be rented to pilgrims show that, like Shemitah produce, it belongs to no one.
The twelve weekday requests of Shemoneh Esrei correspond to the twelve working tribes, while on Shabbos, Yaakov's day, one asks only for spiritual needs.
Shemitah turns every Jew into a Kohen, who has no portion of land and whose portion is Hashem.
Because Shemitah is itself a tosefes, an extension of Yerushalayim, the Torah teaches the law of adding to Shemitah, and from it one sees that Shabbos too has a tosefes.
Onkelos's rendering of Yaakov's 'bow' as tefillah shows that the Jewish bow of tefillah is what overcomes Yishmael, the archer, and Kislev's mazal of the bow makes it the time for it.
Shavuos is one day but really a whole week, the eighth week above nature, which is why its offerings may still be brought all seven days.
One who violated Shemitah loses his bond to Shabbos, so Shabbos feels to him like a prison; that is why Shemitah cannot free him and only Yovel can.
The Torah was given in forty days, the mem of 'mishpacha'; a Jew who loses it is left with 'shifcha', and Yovel restores him to the mishpacha.

Counting the nineteen 'geulos' of Behar against Shemoneh Esrei, the redemption of the man sold to the idol falls on the twelfth, the bracha against heretics, and the one who redeems him on the thirteenth, the bracha of the tzaddikim.
The soul of Malchus Beis David was hidden among Moav like a diamond in a garbage can, where the Satan would never think to look.
The Rav suggests, saying he has not seen it in a sefer, that the parsha of Yovel is written in Beis Lechem Yehudah, which explains why Rus returned there and why Rachel is buried there.
The Rashbam's 'forever' does not argue with the halachah; it describes what a servant who refused Shemitah deserves, and Yovel rescues him anyway.

The Ramak teaches that the fiftieth mention of Yetzias Mitzrayim in the Torah, which stands for the coming of Mashiach, is not the fiftieth in order but the one right after the tochachah in Bechukosai.
The 49 curses of the tochachah can be seen as the 49 gates of galus, with the fiftieth gate, the end of galus, following immediately after.

Jews keep even mitzvos given to the Avos, like milah and gid hanasheh, only because Moshe Rabbeinu commanded them, since belief in Moshe rests on Hashem appointing him before the whole nation at Sinai.
The laws of nature are themselves a Torah: a bird flies and a tree grows because Hashem commanded it, and He breaks nature only rarely, as one would set aside a mitzvah only when truly needed.
Shemitah is a Har Sinai that never ended: Matan Torah was a one-time open miracle, while Shemitah defies nature in Eretz Yisrael in every cycle for all to see.
The Torah's willingness to promise things that every Jew could test, like the safety of the land during the pilgrimages, is itself a proof that it comes from Hashem.
The Rav reads the law of gravity as the Torah's principle that everything returns to its origin: earth falls to the earth, fire rises to its source, and the neshamah rises to where it came from.

A shidduch has two origins: the isha's origin in the ish, and the origin of that origin, Adam's in the earth of the mizbeach. Therefore one cut off from his wife is cut off from Eretz Yisrael, which the Rav sees in the first Mishnah of Gittin speaking of a get from outside the land.

The difference between the daughters of Tzelafchad and Nadav and Avihu: the daughters were tzidkaniyos whose heart was a true magnet; it drew them to no one because their match was tied to a nachalah not yet given, and the moment it was given they married their nearby cousins without being choosy.
Land in Eretz Yisrael returns at Yovel because a field is bound to its owner's neshamah and his portion of Torah; what was bought belongs to someone else's neshamah and must go back to its origin.

Gilad is the land of return: Eliyahu, herald of the final Yovel, chose to live there, and like Amalek it could be conquered only by Rachel's children, the neshamah of return, which is why Moshe left it for Machir.
Moshe's explaining the Torah in seventy languages prepared the people for the seventy levels of galus, so that the Torah would reach down with them into the lowest one.
Adam is the 'challah of the world': Hashem plucked his earth out of the place of the Mizbeach as a woman plucks challah from her dough, and Chava in turn is the challah plucked out of Adam.
The shisin, the cavity under the Mizbeach into which the wine of nesachim flows, is the very hole left where Hashem took out Adam's earth.
Newton described gravity but not its reason; the reason is that everything came from the earth and is drawn back to its source, the same law that makes a marriage a reunion rather than a union.
The sotah is tested with dust from the Mikdash, and the Mizbeach weeps at a divorce, because husband and wife were once together in the dust beneath the Mizbeach.

Gittin opens with a get sent from overseas to Eretz Yisrael because a man's land and his wife are one source; being cut off from one is being cut off from the other, which is also why the Gemara of the Churban is in Gittin.
Wine, which brings simcha, is poured into the very place from which Adam was taken, to bring joy back to the source that the spies saddened by their unfaithfulness.
The real novelty of 'the last forty days were in favor' is not the first forty days but that after the sin a new time of favor came into being.
Shimon HaTzaddik's resting place is a place of favor less because of the place or the time than because of the soul of the tzaddik buried there.
Until the exile of Bavel the Written Torah was taught together with the received laws from Moshe, but the pilpul, chiddushim and toil of the Oral Torah began with Shimon HaTzaddik.
Each week of the seven consolations reflects one of the seven middos; this week is tiferes, which is Torah, and the haftarah's call to water and its ending with Hashem's glory show it.
From the Akeidah the Rav learns that a trial is what brings out yiras Shamayim, so the trials of this generation are its path to fear of G-d.
The Rav treats getting used to Eretz Yisroel as a real spiritual danger that calls for deliberate, ongoing renewal.
Daily davening about Yerushalayim can serve as an indirect tool to refresh one's love for the land.
The same words of prayer for Yerushalayim mean something different to one who lives nearby: he feels close where a Jew abroad feels distant.
The parable of the log and the planted tree: mere presence in the land decays, while being rooted through Torah brings growth.
Even the most ordinary acts, like washing negel vasser or greeting a Jew, become many times holier when done in Eretz Yisrael.
A shared davening is built when each person contributes his own spark to the common flame.
Love for one's own chavurah takes precedence over the general love of every Jew, because those close by come first, as the Ba'al Shem Tov's talmidim taught.
The worsening situation of the Jews is itself read as a preparation for miracles, so the response is for each to do his part.
Eretz Yisroel stands to the world as Rosh Hashana to the year and Shabbos to the week: it is the root from which everything draws, and Yerushalayim is the Shabbos within it.
In Eretz Yisroel a Jew receives a neshama from a higher Name, like the neshama yeseira of Shabbos; like a wire carrying higher voltage, it makes both his mitzvos and his sins far greater.
Because the land is surrounded by water on all four sides, entering it is like immersing in a mikveh before Shabbos.
The kedusha of Eretz Yisroel exceeds that of a beis haknesses, since even inside a shul one must turn one's heart toward the land.
In Eretz Yisroel the yetzer hara is greater too: the one abroad is only its messenger, since whoever is greater has a greater yetzer.
Moshe Rabbeinu, at home in heaven, first needed to open with praise in the land of Sichon and Og, because the kedusha of Eretz Yisroel there awed him more than heaven itself.
Measured as land, Eretz Yisroel is a small territory; measured as a diamond, it is enormous.
The Rav reads the Rebbe Reb Elimelech's words to the penitent as showing that the hardship of the road itself does much of the work of teshuvah, before one even reaches the tzaddik.
Guarding one's eyes on the plane is not only a defense; the Rav calls it a greater preparation, since one sees Tziyon according to the eyes one brings to it.

Walled-city Purim was tied to Yehoshua bin Nun precisely because Yerushalayim lay in ruins at the time of the miracle; the day was set to give it honor, so coming there for Purim reaches the day's true intent.

The geulah did not come through the great Tanna'im, Amora'im and Rishonim; for His own reasons Hashem wants it to come through small people, so perhaps the small efforts of those preparing for Yerushalayim will bring it.

The Rav compares the longing for Eretz Yisroel to a healthy appetite: the Avos' desire was healthy, so it went to the true good, and a Jew who lacks that longing has spoiled his desire, like one who ate something sour and lost his appetite.

Yerushalayim is the place of unity because it is the concentration of all Eretz Yisroel; therefore baseless hatred meant exile from it, and one without unity does not belong in Yerushalayim, just as he does not belong in Purim.
When a holy place leaves one unmoved, the Rav applies the Ba'al Shem Tov's advice for a closed heart in davening: keep working with emunah, and the feeling will come as a gift after the toil.
Since the exile came from despising the desirable land, the inner work of the Three Weeks is to repair that sin by valuing Eretz Yisroel and rejoicing in it.
Great tzaddikim were held back from reaching Eretz Yisroel by Heaven, because their tefillos at the gate of heaven would have hastened the geulah while the exile still had to continue.
Following Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, the meraglim's report came from seeing by ruach hakodesh the generations that would fall in the land, since its yetzer hara is as great as its holiness.
The Yamim Tovim, which give a Jew his emunah and life for the whole year, depend on the months being fixed by Jews in Eretz Yisroel, so without a Jewish settlement there Klal Yisroel could not exist.
Moshe Rabbeinu could not abolish the yetzer hara for avodah zarah, while Yehoshua and the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah could, because only they had the merit of entering Eretz Yisroel.
Rashi read 'better one day in Your courts than a thousand' as a thousand years because, as a holy man, he knew what Eretz Yisroel is worth.
Moshe Rabbeinu mentions Eretz Yisroel again and again in Sefer Devarim because speaking about the land, like speaking about tzaddikim, brings yiras shamayim.
The Rav reads Rashi's 'as if given to you today' as the measure for the love of the land: it must burn with the freshness of a new gift.
From 'goy echad ba'aretz' he derives that Jews are one nation only in Eretz Yisroel; outside it a Jew is like an animal pacing in a zoo, in a place where he does not belong.
He warns that Jerusalem can become like the daily breakfast oatmeal one stops noticing; a visit there needs freshness and preparation.
He explains 'Shabbos Chazon' from the word chazah, seeing: the vision of the third Beis HaMikdash is seen with the heart, not the eyes.
He connects Beis Lechem, Rachel's place, with Yovel, the return of each man to his inheritance, so that 'veshavu vanim ligvulam' is its fulfillment.

He traces galus to jealousy rooted in the moon's diminishing, through Kayin, the brothers and Yeravam to the hatred that destroyed the Beis HaMikdash, and says Rachel, the aspect of the moon, began its repair by overcoming jealousy.
Whatever exists in time exists in place: the softer judgment of the second day of Rosh Hashanah, the aspect of Rachel, has its place all year at Kever Rachel.
Leah is the aspect of harsh judgment and Rachel of soft judgment, which the Rav maps onto the first and second days of Rosh Hashanah.
Though Yirmiyahu is the prophet of lament, the Rav says no comfort in all of Yeshayahu, the prophet of comfort, is as great as the haftorah of the second day of Rosh Hashanah.
Shmuel's fifty-two years and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's eighteen add up to seventy, which is why, as his gilgul, he said he was 'like seventy years old'.
Because Shmuel never took benefit from anyone, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, his gilgul, could not be supported as nasi by others and needed his own wealth.
Every generation has its own 'counsel of the spies', changing shape like a cloud; in this generation it is kefirah, pritzus and electronic devices.
Above, Hashem Himself looks at the hidden sod of each Jew, which no one else sees, and that sod is good.
Rachel's burial on the road is read through the contrast of home and road: the home gathers, the road scatters, so the akeres habayis had to lie on the road to bring her gathering power into exile.
Had Rachel been buried in a closed cave like the other Avos and Imahos, the Jews in exile would have had no way back, since they could not reach her.
Sefer Devarim is the seventh book and the kallah, as Shabbos is the seventh day and the kallah, which is why it is begun on Shabbos Chazon.
The barrenness the kever of Shmuel and Chana can heal is also spiritual: Torah and tefilah without siyata dishmaya are 'barren' and bear no fruit.
Shmuel embodies kingship for both lines of Klal Yisrael, anointing Shaul from Rachel and David from Leah.

Eretz Yisroel is to place what Shabbos is to time: the 'eretz chemdah' parallels the 'chemdas hayamim', and just as a blatt Gemara on Shabbos is holier and a sin on Shabbos graver, in Eretz Yisroel both merit and damage are magnified.

Using the Arizal's reason for the second day of Yom Tov abroad, a smaller neshamah that cannot absorb the light in one day, the Rav explains that the light of Shabbos Purim in Yerushalayim is so great that even a Jew of Eretz Yisroel needs three days to receive it.

Moshe Rabbeinu, though far greater, could not pray away the yetzer hara of avodah zarah because he was outside the land, while Yehoshua and, a thousand years later, the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah could, through the power of tefillah in Eretz Yisroel.

Although residency in Eretz Yisroel normally requires thirty days, one day of Purim in Yerushalayim makes a person a resident of a walled city, just as seven days of Sukkos count as dwelling because the sukkah defines dwelling.

Mordechai and Esther originally instituted reading the Megillah even on Shabbos; only later was it moved, for the honor of Shabbos. Therefore the whole power of Purim in Yerushalayim rests in its Shabbos even though the Megillah is not read then.
The earth of Eretz Yisroel is holier than the heavens of chutz la'aretz; seeing it as ordinary land is like seeing a Jew and a goy as the same person because their bodies look alike.

A tefillah without feeling can be greater than one with it: R' Avraham Kalisker concluded that his first dry tefillah in the land surpassed the famous minchah under the tree, since the feeling is a gift and the labor is the avodah.
Rochel's 'disgrace' that Hashem took away at Yosef's birth is read as the disgrace of orlah: against Esav, who was never circumcised, came Yosef, born circumcised, the foundation of the bris.

The mazal of Elul, the maiden, was created when a maiden grabbed an angel's wing to escape corruption; Elul is therefore a month of 'grabbing', a time to seize every opportunity and fly upward in prayer.
Although Yishmael is circumcised, he counts as 'arel': milah is meant to weaken desire, and he is the greatest ba'al ta'avah, so the 'arel v'tamei' that may no longer enter Yerushalayim includes him.

Kalev's lone stand against the spies, who claimed to be the majority and the heads of Bnei Yisrael, is the model for today's test: holding to true views alone against a whole world drawn after false leaders.
Because every prayer passes through the place of the Avos, Shemoneh Esrei opens by binding the tefillah to 'the G-d of Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov'.
Tu B'Av, the full moon, is the root of the joy of chassan and kallah between Hashem and Knesses Yisrael that will be complete at Shemini Atzeres and with Mashiach.
The Rav reads 'matzeves kevuras Rachel ad hayom' as meaning that the very lights Yaakov and the shevatim placed in the matzeivah are still present there today.

The thirteenth of Adar is a 'zman kehilah', and gathering in unity at Rachel, the one who unites Klal Yisroel, means gathering at the very root of kehilah, whose light is to be carried into the days of Purim.
Purim, carrying the aspect of Moshiach ben Yosef and the war with Amalek, is followed by Nissan, the aspect of Moshiach ben Dovid and the Beis Hamikdash.
Rachel's two acts of mesirus nefesh map onto two redemptions: Yosef stands for Moshiach, and Binyamin, the root of Mordechai, stands for Purim.

Through bechirah and yediah the Rav reconciles the Zohar's demand that Rachel's grave be uncovered with its being built over: had it been a matter of choice it should not have been done, but since nothing happens without Hashem's will, it shows that her grave must now be covered.
That even Rachel, the revealed one, is now hidden behind walls upon walls shows the lowest level of hester, which is exactly what Purim, the megillah of hester, comes to uncover.
Rachel and Lavan's sheep form one theme: the mother of the exiled souls and the souls themselves, so Yaakov's rolling the stone was an act of easing their exile.
The well is Knesses Yisrael, and the stone Yaakov rolled off it is a weight lifted from the Jewish heart in exile.
Yaakov's seven years of work for Rachel were the time the souls still needed in Lavan's captivity before they could pass from Rachel to Yaakov.
Rachel's death on reaching Eretz Yisrael marks the end of her task, and her burial on the road prepares her to take it up again in later exiles.
The shepherds' words that Rachel comes with the sheep were a sign that the time had come for the souls to be handed to Yaakov and turned from sheep into six hundred thousand Jewish souls.
Since Rosh Hashanah is 'the day the world is conceived', the place where Chana conceived Shmuel, the first of the prophets, carries the quality of Rosh Hashanah.

Eli's objection shows that the merit of a long tefillah was not yet known; it was Chana who introduced it, and tefillah remains something people belittle, though honor is shown for Torah and tzedakah.
Barrenness can be spiritual: a tefillah that is not answered, or learning without success, has no fruit, and the place where Chana's barrenness ended is a segulah against it.
Shmuel's first prophecy, the punishment of Chofni and Pinchas for keeping women from returning to their families, served to remove barrenness from Klal Yisroel.
Chana used the name Tzevaos, never found in the Chumash, to ask for children, because Tzevaos means the hosts of Jewish souls; and with Shmuel began the prophets' nourishment from netzach and hod.
The word 'vehaya' in 'vehaya ki hirbisa lehispallel' hints that Chana's tefillah was on Rosh Hashanah, since vehaya is the form tied to the month of Tishrei.

Just as Hashem made six days and a seventh that is Shabbos, among the lands the seventh is Eretz Yisroel: it is the Shabbos of geography, and like Shabbos one can be inside it without any connection to it.
Rosh Hashanah judges once a year because it heads the year in time; Eretz Yisroel, created first, is the head in place, so there one is judged every day.
The Torah that Moshe wrote begins with Eretz Yisroel, per Rashi on Bereishis, and ends with Hashem showing him the land, so Eretz Yisroel encompasses the whole Torah.
Moshe asked to be able to pray only when standing at the edge of Eretz Yisroel, not during forty days in heaven, because the ground of Eretz Yisroel is holier than the heaven above chutz la'aretz.
Eretz Yisroel is called 'wide' though it is small, as a walnut-sized diamond is huge while a room-sized plot in Manhattan is tiny: its greatness is measured by its preciousness.
Water surrounds Eretz Yisroel on all four sides so that one immerses and purifies oneself before entering the land.
The sea fled and the mountains danced away at Matan Torah not out of awe but because their gashmiyus blocked their natural pull to Hashem, the way clay between a magnet and iron stops the attraction.
The word Shabbos carries two meanings, stopping and returning, and they are one: by stopping work a person returns to his root.

Osniel ben Kenaz could restore the 3,000 forgotten halachos because the land he conquered corresponded to them; owning the land made him master of the halachos rooted in it, showing that derash is the depth of pshat.

The mizbeach weeps specifically over divorcing a first wife because husband and wife were one soul at the place of the mizbeach, from where Adam was formed, so it alone feels the pain of their separation.
Yom Kippur and Shavuos are both the fiftieth: on Yom Kippur a Jew rises to heaven and lives like an angel, while on Shavuos heaven comes down and even chametz becomes an offering.
The women were told first at Sinai to show that the Torah was given as a complete union between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, which follows no order of rank and no reckoning, and which no sin can break.
The Rav identifies the four laws Moshe had to ask about as all belonging to Yovel, the fiftieth gate, so that they were given at Sinai yet hidden from Moshe because they stand above all grasp.

Wine stands for the heart's intuition and bread for intellect; matters of Yovel are reached by feeling, which is why women, the daughters of Tzelofchad and the wise woman of Dovid's time, revealed that no Jew is cast off.
The wood-gatherer was liable by the law a beis din must follow, yet in the depth known only to Hashem he was not, since he acted for the sake of Heaven; such judgment belongs to the level of Yovel.

Hashem commanded that the showbread be eaten after nine days, though it looked stale, to teach against the blasphemer's claim that the Jewish camp is 'stale' and mixed, and that every Jew is holy and must be loved.

The Rav reads 'Shulamis' as a passive form: Knesses Yisrael receives the nations' greeting but does not return it or mingle with them, the opposite of Shlomis bas Divri who greeted everyone and lost her son his place in the camp.
Like the four letters of Hashem's Name, the hidden and revealed parts of the Torah are bound together, so whoever learns the revealed Torah receives the hidden within it, even without grasping it.

The Rav treats the Jew, Shabbos and Eretz Yisrael as one distinction in three dimensions: Eretz Yisrael is the 'Jew' of geography and Shabbos the Jewish day, a different reality altogether, not a better version of the same thing.
Shemitah comes every seventh year rather than every seventh day because the land lives on a slower clock than a person.
The Chasam Sofer's no-eating in yovel follows from yovel being the land's Yom Kippur and Shavuos; Moshe went without food on Sinai because he was in the world of yovel.
Osniel ben Kenaz could restore forgotten halachos by winning Kiryas Sefer, because every spot in Eretz Yisrael is bound to a particular halachah; the land is a Sefer Torah.
Boaz's renewal of the halachah permitting a Moabite woman, together with the field he acquired with Rus, parallels Osniel: a halachah renewed together with a field that belongs to it.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is a soul of yovel, which is why the halachah follows him in the laws of Shabbos, and why his view that one should only learn will become halachah in the time of yovel.
A thief's punishment of being sold fits his sin: lacking bitachon he took what was not his and cut himself off from his own root in the Torah, so he is made to eat from a root that is not his.
Shemitah and yovel are not merely one example of Torah from Sinai: their structure of seven sevens and the fiftieth is the very structure of Sefirah and Shavuos, so they embody what Sinai is.
Yerushalayim is to place what Shabbos is to time: Hashem's private domain inside the world, which is why its houses were not rented and nothing was planted there, making it an endless shemitah.

The twelve tribes, the twelve months and the twelve middle blessings of Shemoneh Esrei are all 'weekday' concepts, while Yaakov Avinu, the trunk from which the twelve branches grow, is the Shabbos above them.

There are three levels: weekday (the tribes, Eretz Yisrael), Shabbos (shemitah, Yerushalayim, the kohen), and yovel (the Beis HaMikdash, the Kohen Gadol, Yom Kippur, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai), the last being above time and place.

The holiness of Eretz Yisrael came through human conquest and could be undone, like Rosh Chodesh which needs a beis din; the holiness of Yerushalayim, like Shabbos, comes from the Shechinah and is never annulled.
The Aron taking no space is not counted among the ten miracles of the Mikdash because in the Kodesh HaKodashim, which is above place, this is simply its nature.

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who held that one should learn constantly, is 'Shabbos' for whom every weekday is Shabbos, and indeed 'Shabbos of Shabbosos', the fiftieth, which is why his day carries the light of Shavuos.
The Rav calls the count to yovel 'a Xerox copy' of Sefiras HaOmer: seven sabbaths of years then the fiftieth year, as seven weeks then the fiftieth day, so Shavuos is a yovel.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is like Hashem, who is G-d for everyone: as Rebbe he demands no shtreimel, kapote or beard, because he sees the secret in every Jew.
The Torah says 'eiker' because avodah zarah itself will be uprooted, yet the Jew sold to it will be rescued: the uprooting is for the idol, the redemption for the Jew.
The 'ends of the heavens' teaches that even the most distant Jew is still bound to the last step of heaven, which goes with him wherever he is cast.
Shifchah and mishpachah share a root meaning attachment: the shifchah is attached where there is no Torah, and yovel returns each Jew to his true mishpachah, rooted in Eretz Yisrael and Matan Torah.

In the holiest places the klipah is strongest: Beis Lechem, place of Mashiach, became the cradle of Christianity, as the site of the Beis HaMikdash and the peak of Har HaCarmel are covered by foreign worship.
The Rav reads Shlomo's words 'Hashem said He would dwell in the thick cloud' as Shlomo's foresight of galus: the same Shechinah that filled the Mikdash would remain among Jews in hiding.
The Machpelah is an extension of the Mikdash; they had to be in two places because if the avos lay in Yerushalayim, the churban would have touched the place of their hidden presence.
Chevron is the opposite of churban: churban means cut off, Chevron means joined, so even when Yerushalayim lies in ruins, one remains connected to the avos through the Machpelah.
The Machpelah is the 'hester within hester' that the Ba'al Shem Tov feared, yet even there the avos are alive and pray for the Jews.
Ornan, the other name of Aravna, equals 'aish' (fire) in gematria, while Efron recalls 'afar' (earth): the Mikdash is fire that can be extinguished, the Machpelah earth that never passes.
Had Rachel, who embodies revelation, been buried in the Machpelah, she would have brought light into the place of concealment and galus could not have existed.
Parshas Vayeira ends with revelation at the Akeidah and Chayei Sarah follows at once with the Machpelah, where Hashem and the avos are not seen.

The Rav reads the bringing of bikkurim as a po'el dimyoni: the seven species stand for seven kinds of Jews, and carrying them to Yerushalayim with song is a symbolic act that assures the exiles will be brought back the same way.
Chazal chose Arami oved avi for the telling of the Exodus because it contains the fiftieth mention of the Exodus in the Torah, which carries the power of the final redemption from the fiftieth gate.

Rosh Hashana is the Beis Hamikdash in time: as the world spread out from the place of the Mikdash, the whole year spreads out from Rosh Hashana, and on it the Mikdash comes to the Jew rather than the Jew going to the Mikdash.
Since time is higher than place, the destroyers of the Mikdash ruled only over its place; the sanctity of Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur and Shabbos, the Mikdash in time, remained beyond their reach.
There is no aliya l'regel on Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur because the Mikdash then comes to every Jew, which is why one bows fully on Yom Kippur even today, 'before Hashem'.
Death entered the world as aging, the loss of freshness; chaim means freshness, and the Mikdash, the place of reishis, is where aging and sleep had no hold.
A fruit that ripens before all others holds a precious soul with zerizus, so it belongs in the place of reishis, and the owner gives it to the Kohen as his messenger to elevate it.

Learning Torah about Eretz Yisrael is not like reading a description of a food one has never tasted: because the Torah is Toras chaim and comes from the same root as the land, the learning itself gives the taste and the bond.
Eretz Yisrael is small only to one who measures it as real estate; like a diamond, whose value is not in its size, it is the land for whose sake the world and the Torah were made.

The true 'tziyunim' of the pasuk 'set up signposts' are not those who live in the land without the Torah, but the Jews who keep the Torah in chutz laaretz; calling others by that name is a misuse of the word.

The Mishnah of the shomrim may say 'hen' (they are), but the avos nezikin cannot carry a word of being, because they stand against Hashem's Name and have no permanence; that is also why a Mishnah about them can be 'not upheld'.

The quarrel between the shepherds of Avraham and of Lot was not a by-product of the surrounding strife but a protective hatred Hashem placed between the followers of a tzaddik and a rasha, so the tzaddik would not be harmed by bad company.

Tidal 'king of nations' is Edom, which unlike the other kingdoms is a mixture of all nations; Edom's last tactic, like Esav's kiss, is to harm through friendship and joining rather than through the bite.

Each episode of the parsha, from Lot through the money of Sedom and Yishmael to milah, is one more stage of the single program of 'Lech lecha': cutting away what is not oneself to reach the pure root.
Yerushalayim is in a constant state of shemitah, and the seventh year is not a new holiness but Yerushalayim overflowing onto all of Eretz Yisrael.
Yaakov, the trunk of the tree, is Shabbos and the tribes are the weekday Roshei Chodesh; so Eretz Yisrael was divided among the tribes, while Yerushalayim, belonging to the trunk, was not.
In shemitah every Jew becomes like a Levi or kohen without a field, a foretaste of the World to Come when all Jews will be kohanim.
Since shemitah itself is a tosefes on Yerushalayim, every tosefes in the Torah, even tosefes Shabbos, is learned from shemitah.
Rabbi Akiva, a descendant of converts who are an addition to Klal Yisrael, is the one who expounded the crowns added to the letters and who taught tosefes from shemitah.
A Jew who enters the sukkah after Yom Kippur is like a convicted man who flees to Eretz Yisrael, where the verdict is reopened and Hashem Himself judges with mercy.
Ki Savo, read before Rosh Hashanah, is a mussar on the 122 days of the past year that were not used, while Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu hint at the 122 days now beginning.

Shemitah is not a new state that appears every seven years; it is the permanent shemitah of Yerushalayim overflowing its banks for one year over all of Eretz Yisrael, so that the whole land becomes Yerushalayim and every Jew a kohen.

Because shemitah as a whole is tosefes, the law of adding to holy times is learned specifically from it, and by Rabbi Akiva, a descendant of converts who were themselves an 'addition' to Israel and who expounded the crowns added to the letters.

The aron taking no space was not counted as a miracle because in the Kodesh HaKodashim, where heaven meets earth, being above measure is simply heaven's nature; the same idea explains why the fiftieth year can count for two cycles.

At the end of every Shabbos and every shemitah there is a 'doubt in heaven' whether what follows will be a new first or the eighth, which is why Moshiach is expected then, why melave malka belongs to David, and why chassidic rebbes extended shalosh seudos past Shabbos.
'Magen David' is said only in the haftarah blessings after maftir, the eighth aliyah, because David's true greatness, beyond the Avos, belongs to the eighth world and cannot yet be grasped.

The king, Yerushalayim and Yom Kippur are the heart of soul, place and time; at Hakhel in the eighth year the king stands in Yerushalayim at the turn of the year, and this is why the Rambam describes Hakhel as hearing the Torah as at Sinai.

The Rav sees the rebuilding of the Old City's twisting streets exactly as before, done by an engineer for historical reasons, as Hashem steering him so that Yerushalayim below would match Yerushalayim above.
The Gemara's reason for the name Teveria shows, according to the Rav, that Chazal knew a holy city's name is never random, even when a wicked ruler gave it.
He reads the name Yerushalayim as a joining of Yir'eh and Shalem, which in turn is the joining of service of G-d with peace between people that no other place achieves.
The pilgrimage, in the Rav's reading, raised each tribe from its own portion to the level of Yaakov, the trunk of the tree, which is why Yerushalayim was never divided among the tribes.
The Rav links the 'shivtei Kah' to the miracles of Yerushalayim: carrying the Name Kah, the tribes are raised above place, time and calculation.

He answers the Brisker Rav's question on the closing of the brachah for Yerushalayim by saying that David is Yerushalayim, since the Davidic kings are so nullified to it that they are the city itself.
